parts.title: If You Had to Watch a Stone for Five Minutes, Would Your “Bad-Guy Switch” Turn On?
parts.part1:
A stone. Still a stone. Surely something will happen soon—but no, it’s a stone. Nothing happens on the screen. This goes on for five minutes. But you, the viewer, can still do one thing: make someone else’s reward smaller.

This suddenly sounds dark. But it comes from an online experiment with people in the United States. They were put into groups at random. One group watched a five-minute video of a stone, where nothing happened. The other group watched a magician.

During the video, they had three choices. They could make another person’s reward smaller, make it bigger, or do nothing. They could change it by 10 cents each time, up to 50 cents in all. The stone on the screen stayed quiet, while the viewers were given “a little power.”

So, did boredom become fuel for being mean?
parts.part2:
People who strongly liked seeing others suffer were more likely to make the other person’s reward smaller after watching the stone video than after watching the magician video. For people who felt this less strongly, there was no clear difference.

You may want to say, “So, it really depends on personality.” But there is more to the story.

In the next experiment, people were again put into groups at random. But this time, they could not make the reward bigger. They could only make it smaller. This time, it did not matter how strongly people liked seeing others suffer. People who watched the stone video were more likely to make another person’s reward smaller than people in the other groups.

If we look only at personality, we may miss something. We need to ask not only what kind of person someone is, but also what they can do in that situation. We thought we were reading a profile of the person. Now we also notice how the stage is set.
parts.part3:
But it is too soon to say, “Add a button to make rewards bigger and bring world peace!” The two were separate experiments. We cannot say the choices alone caused the different results. We do not know if giving people a choice to make rewards bigger can stop meanness.

The experiment looked only at brief boredom. It also looked only at actions that made another person’s reward smaller. We cannot use its results directly to explain everyday meanness or boredom that lasts a long time.

Even so, we see boring moments a little differently now. We can ask not only, “What mustn’t I do?” but also, “What else can I do instead?” Before we look at someone’s personality, we can look at the menu in front of us. The stone may not move for five minutes. But the question we ask changes a little.
parts.in_one_line: Stone-watchers were more likely to make another person’s reward smaller. In one test, this was true only for people who strongly liked seeing others suffer; in another, it was true at every level. The tests suggest choices may matter along with personality, but they do not show that offering a choice to make rewards bigger stops meanness or applies to everyday life.

parts.title: If You Had to Watch a Stone for Five Minutes, Would Your “Bad-Guy Switch” Turn On?
parts.part1:
A stone. Still a stone. Surely something will happen soon—no, it’s a stone. Nothing happens on the screen. That goes on for five minutes. But you, the viewer, can still get one thing done: cut someone else’s reward.

This sounds grim all of a sudden, but it’s about an online experiment with participants in the United States. They were randomly assigned to watch either a five-minute video of a stone, where nothing happened, or a video of a magician.

During that time, they had three choices: reduce another participant’s reward, increase it, or do nothing. They could change it by 10 cents at a time, up to a maximum of 50 cents. The stone on the screen stayed silent, while the viewers were handed “a little power.”

So, did boredom become fuel for meanness?
parts.part2:
Participants who were strongly inclined to enjoy seeing others suffer were more likely to reduce the other person’s reward after watching the stone video than after watching the magician video. Among those with a weaker tendency, there was no clear difference.

You might want to dismiss this by saying, “So it really is a matter of personality.” But there’s more to the story.

In the next experiment, participants were again randomly assigned to groups. But this time, there was no option to increase the reward. The only choice was to reduce it. This time, regardless of how strongly participants were inclined to enjoy seeing others suffer, those who watched the stone video were more likely to reduce another person’s reward than those in the other conditions.

Well, if we focus only on personality, we may miss something. Along with “what kind of person someone is,” there’s also “what they can do in that situation.” We thought we were reading a profile of the person, but now we start noticing the stage setup, too.
parts.part3:
But it’s too soon to jump to “Add a button to increase rewards and bring world peace!” The two were separate experiments. We can’t say that the difference in choices alone caused the difference in results. We don’t know that offering an “increase” option can prevent meanness.

The experiment also dealt only with brief boredom and actions that reduced another person’s reward. We can’t apply its findings directly to everyday meanness or boredom that lasts a long time.

Even so, our view of boring moments shifts a little. We can ask not only “What mustn’t I do?” but also “What else can I do instead?” Before looking into someone’s personality, look at the menu in front of us. The stone may not move for five minutes, but the question we ask shifts a little.
parts.in_one_line: Stone-watchers were more likely to cut another person’s reward—only those high in sadistic tendencies in one experiment, but people at every level in another. The findings suggest that the choices available in a situation may matter alongside personality. But these separate, brief experiments do not show that offering an increase option prevents meanness or that the findings apply to everyday life.
